name: Drama and Performance
title: Drama and Performance
answer: AI can serve drama and performance in two ways: as a rehearsal partner that reads scene lines so a student can practice timing, memorization, and delivery at home, and as a drafting aid for the production's administrative work, such as rehearsal schedules, prop lists, and program notes. It matters because it makes more practice possible when a partner is unavailable and frees teacher time for directing, while the creative work of the production stays with the students and the director.

crumbs.name: Arts, Music, Physical Education, and Health

sections.body: Actors need scene partners, and a partner is not always available. A voice tool can read the other lines in a scene so a student can rehearse at home, practicing timing, memorization, and delivery. The tool cannot give the kind of feedback a director or fellow actor provides, but it makes more practice possible. On the production side, drafting rehearsal schedules, prop lists, and program notes takes time that could go into directing, and an approved tool can produce first drafts that the teacher edits. The creative work of the production stays with the students and the director.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In rehearsal, a student uses a voice tool to read the other lines in a scene so they can practice timing, memorization, and delivery at home when a scene partner is not available. The tool does not replace the feedback a director or fellow actor gives, but it adds practice repetitions. For the business side of a production, teachers can use an approved tool to produce first drafts of rehearsal schedules, prop lists, and program notes, which the teacher then edits, so more time goes into directing. Students writing their own scenes follow the authorship rule: they might use AI to brainstorm a situation or check that dialogue sounds natural, but the script should be the student's own. Any AI help should be disclosed, especially for scripts entered in competitions, and students should know the competition rules before they begin.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It rests on practice rather than research, describing what a voice tool can and cannot do in rehearsal and how an approved tool can produce first drafts for a teacher to edit.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The tool cannot give the kind of feedback a director or fellow actor provides, so it supplements rather than replaces human direction. The creative work of the production stays with the students and the director, and the teacher edits any AI-generated first drafts of schedules, prop lists, or program notes. For student-written scenes, the script should be the student's own, and any AI help should be disclosed, especially for scripts entered in competitions. Students should know the competition rules about AI use before they begin.
